speakeroldname: Hon. Jean-Luc Pepin (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: INTERNATIONAL GRAINS ARRANGEMENT-DISCUSSIONS TO STABILIZE PRICING AND MARKETING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the International Grains Arrangement entered into force on July 1, 1968 at a time when international prices were under some pressure. It was recognized at the outset that it would take some time and a considerable measure of restraint to achieve effective operation of the price provisions of the arrangement. Progress was made in this direction, encouraged by frequent meetings both among exporters and within the International Wheat Council. Canada has consistently observed the minimum prices established for Canadian grades of wheat.
In recent weeks there has been a significant deterioration in prices for high quality wheats traded in European markets. In some instances and for certain grades and classes these prices have been substantially below established I.G.A. minimums, and a significant volume of business has been done by our competitors.
I went to Washington on March 11 and met with senior officials of the department of state and with the Secretary of Agriculture to see if a greater degree of co-operation in pricing matters could not be achieved. The results of these talks hold some promise for the future, but in the present competitive situation 29180-420
amongst exporters it is not likely that immediate restoration of price levels can be achieved. In view of this the Canadian Wheat Board has come to the conclusion that it must meet the competition in the marketplace.
A meeting of the Prices Review Committee of the International Wheat Council is taking place next week and an early meeting of exporters has been called to determine actions necessary to restore price stability in keeping with obligations assumed under the arrangement. Canada will exert every effort to improve the degree of international cooperation with respect to prices through the I.G.A. and in discussion with other exporters. It should be noted that the I.G.A. itself provides procedures for temporary adjustments of minimum prices, since relationships between type and qualities of wheat fluctuate with competitive circumstances.
International co-operation in wheat marketing remains a cardinal principle of Canadian policy and while remaining competitive every effort will be made by Canada in consultation with other exporting and with importing countries to improve and strengthen co-operation with respect to prices and the operation of the I.G.A.

maintopic: INTERNATIONAL GRAINS ARRANGEMENT-DISCUSSIONS TO STABILIZE PRICING AND MARKETING
speechtext:
While we welcome the announcement that the Canadian Wheat Board intends to remain competitive with other world grain exporters and that efforts will be made to stabilize prices, I should like to point out that in present circumstances large amounts of Canadian wheat are being sold at prices greatly below those paid by the Wheat Board. We hope this situation will not be allowed to get worse as a result of refusal by the government to accept some reduction at certain times in international prices. This applies not only to wheat prices but also to prices of coarse grain. We have lost several sales because we allowed our competitors to undercut us in this latter market. I hope that in the future there will be some degree of elasticity in pricing so that we may sell our grain and meet the competition from other exporters in the world.

bad news for the western wheat producers. I think this is the first step toward breaking the bad news that the price of wheat is going to be reduced.
The minister quite properly points out that for certain grades and classes of wheat the prices have been substantially below the I.G.A. minimum. He says that a significant volume of business has been done by our competitors. I would have hoped that the minister would have told the house who are the competitors who are breaking the agreement into which Canada, along with other exporting nations, entered.
It is a well known fact, of course, that the United States, during an interim period between the expiry of the International Wheat Agreement and the coming into effect of the International Grains Arrangement, was selling wheat some 18 cents a bushel below the minimum, despite the fact that we had the assurance of the former minister of trade and commerce that there was a verbal agreement that all parties concerned would adhere to the minimum set out in the proposed I.G.A. agreement.
I hope the minister will take an early opportunity to give the house some further information as to whether or not these competitors of ours who have been selling below the agreed minimum are members of the I.G.A. and, if so, who they are, or whether these sales have been made by exporting countries who are not members of the I.G.A. I cannot think of any outstanding exporters who are not members of the I.G.A.; therefore, I can only conclude that the I.G.A. agreement has been violated by members who have agreed to certain minima and who are now disregarding the agreement. I think this is a very sad affair and must cause the minister, and certainly the farmers of this country, a good deal of concern.
If the situation continues, I agree that the Canadian Wheat Board has no choice but to adjust its prices to meet world competition. But this will mean disaster for the wheat producing industry of Canada. It will mean hardship for a great many farmers in western Canada. I hope that the meeting the minister has announced will be able to restore some price stability.
I am a little worried about the clause in the minister's statement which indicates that the I.G.A. has provided procedures for making temporary adjustments to minimum prices. Unfortunately, these temporary adjustments tend to become permanent. If we are to have a permanent price decline for the balance of
[Mr. Douglas (Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands).!
the term of this agreement, then this will work great hardship on our wheat producers, and of course on the Canadian economy generally.
I am sure that members of the house in all parts of the chamber will wish the minister well in the meeting that is proposed. I am taking it for granted that the minister will press for an adherence to the minima provided by the I.G.A. agreement, rather than for any temporary reduction in price, if this can possibly be avoided.

maintopic: INTERNATIONAL GRAINS ARRANGEMENT-DISCUSSIONS TO STABILIZE PRICING AND MARKETING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I well understand the disappointment of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) with regard to the international grains market, and especially the wheat market. However, I commend him for keeping the house informed on those problems, and for the efforts which have been made in conjunction with the United States authorities with a view to finding favourable solutions.
Nevertheless, I hope that western grain producers will not be too seriously affected financially by those market difficulties. That shows that even when our production capacities are large enough to help supply food to the whole world, there are problems due to competition between men.
I hope the minister will continue his efforts with the co-operation of the Canadian Wheat Board and all those interested in the matter so that happy solutions will be found and that the western wheat producers will not be affected too severely by the consequences of this competition on the international market.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PERMIT ARMED FORCES VOTE IN BY-ELECTIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to give members of Canada's armed forces a vote in federal by-elections. Military personnel declare their places of natural residence for purposes of general elections and should be permitted to vote in by-elections, when one occurs in the place they have declared as their place of natural residence. There is no provision in the Canada Elections Act giving the right of Canadian Armed Forces personnel to vote in such byelections. This is a denial of a basic right in a free society and I recommend this bill to the house to correct this situation.

speechtext:
that Bill C-178, to amend the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act, the Defence Services Pension Continuation Act, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Superannuation Act, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Pension Continuation Act and the Public Service Superannuation Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in view of the opportunity hon. members have had to study this bill since it was given first reading a week ago, there is not a great deal which I feel I need say by way of general explanation at this time. Full opportunity will be provided for a more detailed explanation when the bill is being reviewed by the committee to which it is intended that it should be referred.
While this is a bill of 51 clauses, amending five acts, hon. members will have noted that the majority of them deal with administrative matters, the removal of anomalies or inconsistencies in the provisions of the acts, and amendments which are consequential upon other legislation which has been enacted since these statutes were last before the house. There are some changes in the benefits, coupled with provision for increases in certain contribution rates under the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Superannuation Act. Advance notice of these increases was given three or four months ago when the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cadieux) and the Solicitor General (Mr. Mcllraith) announced the latest general pay increases for the Canadian Forces and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
Statute Law Amendment Act
The contribution rates have remained fixed under these two pension plans since 1946 and 1949, respectively, despite the various benefit improvements which have been made from time to time. During the same period, the contribution rates for certain male civil servants were increased in 1954, and for all of them in 1960, when substantial improvements were made in the Public Service Superannuation Act. Since 1960, the 6 per cent contribution rate for male civil servants has been higher than that for male members of the Canadian Forces and of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, despite the fact that the latter two groups have the more expensive plan, largely because of the lower retirement age at which they can retire on an immediate full pension. Sixty is the lowest age at which a civil servant can retire on full, immediate pension for a reason other than disability.
The present contribution rates are: 6J per cent for males and 5 per cent for females under the Public Service Superannuation Act, 6 per cent for both sexes under the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act, and 6 per cent for males and 5 per cent for females under the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Superannuation Act. In each case these contribution rates represent the combined total for those acts and the Canada Pension Plan or the Quebec Pension Plan as a result of the integration of contributions brought about by the amendments co-ordinating these acts with the Canada Pension Plan in 1966.
Subsequent to those last amendments, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) has tabled reports on the actuarial valuation of the superannuation accounts maintained under the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Superannuation Act. Each of these reports showed the need for an increase in the current rate of contributions. This need arose in part from the amendments which were made in these acts in 1966, including the co-ordination of each of these acts with the Canada Pension Plan.
A combination of this reason, the improvements in benefits proposed in this bill and the lack of any justification for the use of a lower rate of contribution than that under the Public Service Superannuation Act, led the government to couple these proposed increases in the rate of contribution with the last general pay increases for both forces when they were approved. On the other hand, it is proposed to reduce the rate for female members of the Canadian Forces to the 5 per

Statute Law Amendment Act cent payable by female contributors under the other two acts. These contribution changes would take effect on April 1 next.
As far -as benefits are concerned, the most significant changes are proposed under the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act where a substantially new benefit approach is contained in the Bill before the house. Under this provision, a contributor with between 10 and 20 years of service would now have a vested right to a deferred full annuity as well as a discretionary one to an immediate partial annuity in the case of retirement to promote economy or efficiency. As the details of these changes are somewhat complicated, I would prefer to leave any explanation of them until the bill is before the committee.
Amendments are proposed in each of the three superannuation acts which would continue the payment of children's benefits until attainment of the age of 25 if the children are continuing their education on- a basis similar to that provided under the Canada Pension Plan.
There are also minor amendments in all five acts to protect the pension position of a remarried widow of a former contributor when a subsequent marriage terminates in annulment or divorce. Formerly, payment of her pension, which was suspended on remarriage in the usual way, could only be resumed on the death of her next husband.
The last amendment which I should mention this morning has to do with the management of the three superannuation accounts which will remain the responsibility of the Minister of Finance in accordance with the government organization bill.
The present accounting provisions were introduced into these statutes in June of 1965 and slightly amended the following year to reflect the recommendations contained in the report of the Glassco commission. After examining the management of these accounts, the commission reported as follows:
The amounts in these superannuation accounts are not held in cash or invested in securities. Nor should they be, considering that it is the government which is assuming the obligation to pay these pensions. The government utilizes all the moneys for general government purposes, crediting the accounts with interest quarterly for the use of the funds. Normally, the government's contributions, as set forth above, are recorded as budgetary expenditures, but certain deficits, arising out of actuarial valuations in recent years, have been recorded as a deferred charge to be applied against the budgetary revenues of future years.

The related recommendation of the commission reads as follows:
We therefore recommend that a program be authorized by statute to amortize systematically present and future valuation deficits of statutory pension plans by appropriate budgetary charges.
Parliament approved the government's proposals to adopt these recommendations in the statutory amendments of 1965 and 1966. As a result, the government is required to credit to the superannuation accounts in each fiscal year an amount equal to the deficiences which arise from pay increases authorized in that year or are reported in any actuarial valuation report which is laid before parliament in that year. These credits, which are initially made in the form of so-called deferred charges, have to be amortized by budgetary payments in five equal annual instalments commencing in the year in which the deferred charge is credited. These instalments are expected to cost the government in excess of $200 million in this fiscal year.
The government has always recognized that these deficiences, deferred charge credits and resulting budgetary amortization payments would have been substantially smaller if interest had been credited to the account at a higher rate than the 4 per cent which has been payable, at first monthly and more recently quarterly, since the oldest of these accounts came into existence in 1924. Over those years the yield on long-term government bonds has been above, below and now again above this long-term rate of 4 per cent. As answers to parliamentary questions have indicated, up until quite recently the net over-all effect would not have been greatly different had a rate which followed the longterm bond rate been used.
It is not so many years since the government was criticized for crediting interest at a rate which was far too high and thereby being too generous to its employees in comparison with others. Now, of course, the criticism is from the other direction. While it can be shown that the use of an interest rate based on that approved by parliament for the Canada Pension Plan, for example, would not have been sufficient to do away completely with the need for these special contributions, the government recognizes that the validity of the criticism of the 4 per cent rate is realistic at the present time.
The proposed amendments to the accounts sections of the three superannuation acts accordingly contemplate an increase in the
March 14, 1969	COMMONS
interest rate but provide that these higher interest credits are to be applied against the deficiency payments. This is the procedure which would be followed in the operation of a private pension fund which was required to make good deficiencies over a limited period of years under the relevant federal or provincial legislation requiring the solvency of pension funds. While this would substantially reduce, it would not eliminate the special contributions under present conditions.
Here I should point out that these special contributions by the government are in excess of the regular matching contributions for current service which the government has made under the Public Service Superannuation Act and the corresponding regular current contributions under the other two acts. These regular current contributions under the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act and Royal Canadian Mounted Police Superannuation Act have to be even higher than under the Public Service Superannuation Act because of the higher pension cost due to lower retirement ages under those acts. These regular contributions were 10 per cent of pay or one and two-thirds times those of the members of those forces for many years. Accordingly, hon. members will appreciate that, when faced with the need to increase these regular contributions because of benefit improvements over the years, the government felt that the increase required in the current rate of contributions should be shared by the members of those forces, as proposed earlier.
Thus an increase in the interest rate is not expected to create any surplus which would permit a reduction in current contributions or an improvement in benefits. The special contributions which otherwise would have been made will simply be reduced by the amount of the additional interest under present conditions. Nor will it produce a surplus from which an increase in pensions could be paid to those already retired. It will be contended that the government should dip into these funds, pay an increase in pensions nevertheless and leave to the future the question of repaying the new deficit that this would create. But if it did so the statute would require the government to make good this deficiency by budgetary charges, so that this provides no easy way out for the government under the present budgetary position.
Moreover, the government does not propose to abandon the statutory approach recommended by the Glassco commission and brought into force less than four years ago whereby the costs of pensions being earned

Statute Law Amendment Act each year are disclosed to the public and met by the government on a basis which does not leave huge hidden deficits for future taxpayers to meet. The federal and provincial statutes dealing with solvency of private pension funds require certain funding procedures which the government feels it should follow as well.
This brings me to a subject which, as some hon. members have noted, is not included in this bill, namely, amendments to the Public Service Pension Adjustment Act.
Shortly after assuming office, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) stated in response to inquiries that he had arranged for a thorough review of the costs and benefits involved in our social security system in order to have a basis for a reappraisal of the government's policy in this area to ensure that the best use is made of social security payments of all kinds, taking into account the needs of individuals and the economic costs and consequences to the country as a whole. He went on to say that this report would take into account the question of the difficulties now being experienced by those living on pension. The specific question of increasing the pensions of retired public servants was included in this general review to which the Prime Minister referred. The report on this aspect of the review has now been received and is being studied by the government relation to all the other aspects of this broad question. I regret to say that it has not been possible for the government to reach a decision at this time which would permit the inclusion of amendments to the Public Service Pension Adjustment Act in this bill. However, I can assure hon. members that this is continuing to receive active study by the government.
I commend this bill to the house for second reading and referral to committee.

Mr. Speaker, my observations will not be long at this stage of the bill. Obviously, as the minister has said, the bill is one of some considerable complexity and lends itself to more careful and detailed study in the standing committee. I think it is fortunate for us in this house and for the country generally that over the last few years there have been a number of hon. members who, through the medium of committees and their attention to pensions issues of this kind in the public service, have developed a knowledge of the subject and its details that will be most useful when the committee deals with the bill. For that reason I for one am most anxious that
March 14, 1969

Statute Law Amendment Act the bill receive second reading as soon as possible so it can then be sent to the committee. While I think there may be one or two speakers from this party, our observations will in any event not be long and we will certainly not delay second reading of the bill.
As a preliminary observation may I say I am a little puzzled as to why this bill is being sent to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. It seems to me there are other committees more particularly suited to deal with this matter. I think the subject matter of the bill is more relevant to the consideration of other committees. In addition, the Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs has a tremendous amount of work before it and it will have other responsibilities. This bill is long and complicated.
While it is true that under our present system we can exchange personnel to man committees with other people in addition to the regular members, I would have thought it much more advisable to send the bill to a different committee. I sometimes wonder what is the rationale here. What started out as a very excellent idea to break the work of the house down into committees is in fact itself breaking down, and our committee system is not working as it should. For this I must place a lot of the blame on the government.
I shall make one or two observations about the bill, mainly in the hope that the matters I bring up will be considered in the committee. The bill calls for an increase in the contributions of contributors to various pension and superannuation schemes. One thing we will be interested in knowing, and I do not think the minister covered it, is whether there are to be increases in payments from the various pension funds. These have been provided for in the past, and from all indications the funds very greatly exceed the day to day or year to year requirements.
[DOT] (12:20 p.m.)
In speaking of the provisions with respect to the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act it seems to me that here there is a breach of a very solemn undertaking. We become accustomed to breaches of undertaking by this government and to classifying them. A solemn undertaking was given by the former minister of national defence. He said that no serviceman would suffer by reason of voluntary withdrawal following unification. Yet we find that most restrictive interpretations have been imposed on voluntary withdrawals with

a view to discouraging expressions of disapproval of unification by servicemen. Certainly servicemen in many cases have been made prisoners of their pension scheme. The committee could look into this matter and no doubt evidence will be available. What has happened, it seems to me, constitutes a breach of the very solemn undertaking previously given.
I ask the government whether it will not consider R.C.M.P. pensions with respect to those members of the force who retired prior to 1958. So far as I can see the bill brings in no change in this regard. There is a tremendous disparity in present pay scales and scales of superannuation pay between officers and men who have served their full careers in the force. Their pensions are based on pay scales far removed from those applicable today. Tied to the steadily increasing inflation and the effect that has on the limited pensions which these people are receiving, this can only be regarded by hon. members with apprehension and concern.
The same thing applies to public servants who retired prior to 1958. A completely unrealistic comparison has been made, notwithstanding the repeated representations made by hon. members over the years. I pay tribute to hon. members who have done so. Some of them are still here and can speak for themselves. I would not like this occasion to pass without paying tribute to the former member for Carleton, Hon. R. A. Bell, who no longer is a member of the house. Throughout his period in the house he continued making representations with respect to this matter. Other hon. members interested in the subject are still here and I am sure that to them the provisions of the bill constitute a real measure of inequity. No doubt they will deal with that both here and in committee.
I hope the committee will look into the effect of the inauguration of immediate annuities versus deferred annuities as applied previously. This matter is referred to in clause 5 of the proposed bill. We approve the incorporation of active service into regular service in connection with these proposals. This has long been a sore point and we heartily approve of the change. We also approve of clause 35 which gives retired R.C.M.P. personnel the right to treatment allowances similar to those given to disabled veterans.
I thought of dealing with a number of other matters but will not since the bill is to be dealt with in committee. We propose to approve it now on the understanding that we
March 14, 1969	COMMONS
are not approving all aspects of the bill. We are sending it to committee and when it comes back it will be dealt with further.
I end by saying that I regret very much the remarks of the minister to the effect that although the government has possession of the report on increasing the pensions of retired public servants it has not been able to incorporate any proposals or recommendations arising out of it in this bill. The tragedy of inadequate pensions has been with some of our retired civil servants for a great number of years. No target date has been established for implementing the recommendations of the report. This session is to last only two and a half months longer after Easter and, according to the legislative diet the house leader has indicated the government wishes to process, the house will be too busy to deal with the proposals of the report. I am beginning to despair that despite all our good intentions- and we know what the road to hell is paved with-this session will end without anything having been done in this field. No particular legislative proposals will have been brought forward, and it is a matter of great regret to me and other hon. members that this is the case.
That is all I have to say. I hope the bill will pass rapidly through the present stage so that it may receive in committee the attention it deserves and come back to be considered further here.

speechtext:
The
President of the Treasury Board says he is bleeding already. Well, we are making progress.
As I said, a number of provisions in the bill are good and we welcome them. Perhaps I might make it clear that I did not use those words just to say something nice. I like the provision that will make it possible for a widow of a retired civil servant who has married again and had her pension suspended to have that pension reinstated if her second husband runs out on her. As the law now stands, the pension of a widow of a retired civil servant is suspended when she marries a
March 14, 1969

Statute Law Amendment Act second time. If the husband dies she gets it back. If her second husband does not die but there is a divorce, annulment or departure on the part of the husband, she is left without any pension. It is good that we are to have something done about widows caught in that situation. There are not many like that, I believe, but it is good that we are doing something for those who are so caught.
[DOT] (12:30 p.m.)
But what about thousands of widows who do not marry again? Widows of retired civil servants receive pensions which are only 50 per cent of what their husbands' pensions were. Widows of members of parliament get 60 per cent. This is an element of discrimination which I do not think should persist. As a matter of fact, the percentage should be even higher. Something should certainly be done for a widow in the first year after her husband's death when she is trying to maintain the kind of life which they had. At any rate, an improvement is being made and we welcome it.
I notice that the bill provides for the right of a widow on remarriage to commute any value that she is entitled to into a lump sum payment. I think that is good.
I like the provision in the bill that will extend to children of deceased civil servants a pension benefit if those children continue in school or university up to the age of 25. That also is good. This is, of course, another charge on the fund. We are told time and time again the fund cannot afford these extra charges that we propose, but the government does find a few additional charges which it can make on the fund and still carry on. I know there is a difference of degree as well as of kind, but I am looking for some kindness. The minister realizes there are some things which need to be dealt with. I think there are a lot more and I shall come to them in a few minutes.
It is also good that the bill seeks to clarify some ambiguities that existed in relating pensions under these acts to the Canada Pension Plan or the Quebec Pension Plan. For the most part, these are technicalities that the bill clears up. There has also been a distinction made between pensions drawn under the Canada Pension Plan or the Quebec Pension Plan on the basis of retirement and pensions on the basis of a disability. These amendments are all good and we welcome them.
The proposal to have pensions render the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act and the

Royal Canadian Mounted Police Superannuation Act on the same basis as pensions under the Public Service Superannuation Act is a desirable step.
There is one rather major change that is being made by the bill. I have no objection to it, but I think it keeps alive the mythology about pensions that some day we shall have to explode. I refer to the playing around with the fund and the accounting methods. This is not a very professional term to describe what the minister outlined this morning, namely, that provision is being made for a possible increase in the rate of interest to be applied to these funds. The minister did not leave any chance for people to think that this money might be used to pay increased benefits. The minister said precisely that it would not be used for that purpose. He said that in making provision for a higher rate of interest the government is taking the right to cut down the amount of the special contributions that are added from tune to time to keep the fund actuarially in balance.
This is understandable, Mr. Speaker, to anyone who studies this whole subject, but I am sure the minister will not be surprised if some retired civil servants get the notion and even make the charge that the government has done this as a sort of trick, that the government is making provision for the rate of interest to be increased just to show retired civil servants that this is not a way to get increased pension benefits for them. The minister looks at me with a "you know better" expression, but he will have a hard job explaining this to many people. Many people feel that if the government would add one percentage point to the rate of interest, this would provide a sum of money out of which increased benefits could be paid.
A mythology has developed about these pension funds that is highly fictional. We seem to have developed the notion that if money is puit into a fund, somehow, with the interest that is added and so on, there will be money there to pay pensions at a later date which will not cost any one any money. People also have the notion they have a certain right to a pension that they have paid for themselves. The plain fact of the matter is that when people draw pensions they receive a portion of the goods and services being produced today. No matter how many complicated funds are developed, pensions are a pay as you go proposition. People who are retired today are not receiving money which is coming out of a fund. They are not living
March 14, 1969	COMMONS
on goods and services that have been stored. They are receiving money which represents a portion of the goods and services being produced today. In other words, people working today are providing the major part of today's pensions. What is the quid pro quo for the people who are working today? It is that life, society and the government go on and when today's workers retire, the workers of that time will contribute a portion of what they produce to provide a pension for those who are then retired. I am sure the minister agrees with this philosophical part of my remarks as to how pensions operate.
We are trying to kid the troops by having people put money into funds such as the public service superannuation fund and the old age security fund. We try to make people feel they are receiving pensions because they put the money in there, or we try to develop a scheme under which the government can say to people: You cannot get any more because there is not enough money in the fund. I am prepared to admit the logical sequence to this bit of philosophy in which I have been indulging, and it is this: If better pensions are to be paid to people on old age security, people retired from private industry or the civil service, there must be a deliberate decision by the people producing the wealth today that this is to be done.
When I ask the federal government to do something for retired civil servants I am asking for a deliberate decision by a society as affluent as ours. In our society we produce as much as we can and we are able to do this because of the people who preceded us, built up our society and are today retired. The people who are now retired do not receive a decent pension or have a decent standard of living. Retired people in their sixties or seventies should not have only enough to keep up with the cost of living but should be able to enjoy their retirement.
[DOT] (12:40 p.m.)
Because I hold these views about pension funds, I am not as excited about the clauses in this bill that dress up the accounting procedure. I know it will be neater as an accounting proposition to make sure that the fund is actuarially sound, that there is enough there to pay the pensions that have been built up, and so on. It will be nice to be able to say in accounting terms that we are not having to make as heavy charges against current revenues as we would if we were not paying this higher rate of interest, but it all adds up

Statute Law Amendment Act really to just a fine piece of bookkeeping that is far removed from the reality of the situation.
The reality of the situation is that there are retired people today who worked hard to build the country to what it is, whether they were in private industry or in government service. We are now thinking of those who were in government service, who worked hard to build the public service to what it is, to provide the support for the kind of things we try to do in government. Today they are retired and I am sure all those hon. members whose names I have mentioned, in fact all of us in this house, agree that these people ought to have a decent break in terms of pensions today that are not just tied to a fund, not just related to what they were earning 10, 20 or 30 years ago, but are related to what society is able to produce today.
I said initially that I thought there were a number of things in this bill that were good, and I have tried to back up that statement by pointing out those things that I do welcome wholeheartedly. I have spent a moment or two on the question of revamping the fund, not that I think there is anything wrong with it in accounting or bookkeeping terms but rather because I think it is misleading. It keeps alive the mythology that somehow or other these pensions are paid out of the fund.
I remember that some years ago-I think it was 1950-we were discussing in the old age security committee various ways of getting rid of the means test and improving old age pensions. At that time we had an interesting member from Saskatchewan by the name of Ferrie. He was a Liberal. He has passed on and so perhaps I can quote him. We were talking about ways and means of paying a good-sized old age security pension, which in those days meant $40 a month. Dr. George Davidson was the Deputy Minister of Welfare and was the chief witness before our committee. At one point when we got to a question period Mr. Ferrie had a bright idea. He asked, "Could we, by following the funding principle, get to the point where we have put enough money in and do not have to pay any more money in because the interest on the fund will pay the pensions for everyone?" Hon. members know Dr. Davidson. He answered in a very nice, academic way. I mention this incident because it is an illustration of the extreme notions that some people have about pension funds. Pensions are not paid out of anything that is stored up; they are paid out of current production.

The present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp), when he was minister of finance, at one point when we were discussing funds said he agreed with me that we should get on to a pay as you go basis. This is, in fact, what we do. We talk about the public service superannuation fund. Fund? Is that money somewhere? Is it in the Bank of Montreal, in the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, with some trust company, in the Bank of Canada, or anywhere else? No. That fund simply represents figures on the books of the government of Canada. Theoretically the money is there in the consolidated revenue fund, but it is there only in figures on the books.
When the 5 per cent or 64 per cent is deducted from a civil servant's pay, does that mean that so many dollars are actually kept back from his or her pay and put into a fund somewhere? No. It simply means that he gets 934 Per cent of his pay and she gets 95 per cent of her pay and the rest is added to the books in so many figures. I do not quarrel with this procedure but I spell it out to make the point that pensions are a pay as you go proposition and that they represent deliberate choice, and I dare to believe that the other hon. members I have mentioned who will be taking part in this debate agree with me. We are not trying to inveigle the government to do something that is tricky, to play around with the fund. We are straightforwardly and honestly saying that in a society as affluent as ours is in 1969 we have a moral obligation to these people, who helped bring our society to where it is, to give them pension benefits that will enable them to live decent and dignified lives at the present time.
May I now make a point which I have tried to make a good many times, that in this, campaign we are fighting a battle for everyone. Sometimes people will say, and in fact I have received letters asking, "What is all this concern about retired civil servants? What about the rest of the Canadian people?" I point out that we are fighting a battle for everyone. We are trying to get a principle established, to get it started. Perhaps I should not say that because others have done it. There are a number of governments that have brought in pension increase provisions, and there are a number of pension plans in private industry where, usually because of negotiations, there are escalator clauses for the pensions to go up. The auto workers have accomplished a number of these agreements. There is at least

one life insurance company which has a pension plan for its employees that includes an escalator clauses. So it is not a brand new idea. But it is still in its infancy and it is terribly important that we get it started.
Let me talk about this thing in terms of three groups of people. I think we are concerned first of all and rightly so, and in human terms it is important that this is so, for the people who are now retired and who are having a tough time getting by. This applies certainly to those many people who are on lower pension benefits. The figures are on Hansard. I ask for them every year. I have asked for them so often now that I suppose a computer just turns them out, and if the computer is set up to turn them out next year I will ask the same questions again next year.
We are concerned about them, but it is becoming increasingly true that people in the middle and even in the upper brackets, up to the assistant deputy minister and deputy minister levels, who thought when they went out on pensions that the picture was not bad, are also affected. In the meantime, not only have living costs gone up but living standards have changed, and people who had certain professional connections and lived in a certain social milieu find it is not for them any more because the value of their pensions has decreased and they cannot live on their fixed incomes and keep up with the rising standards of living. What is wrong with the desire to do that? We do not expect workers to go 20 years without any increase in wages or salaries. Yet we say to retired civil servants who went out 20 years ago that, but for the small adjustment that some of them got in 1958, this is it; it is a contractual relationship and you are bound by it for life.
In my plea to the minister I am almost prepared to say that we cannot charge the government with breaking any contract so far as the pensions of its retired -civil servants are concerned. Yes, the legalities have been maintained. But the government has broken faith. To me there is a difference and the latter is more important than the former. I think we have broken faith in that we have let these people who have retired get into a position where they have to try to get by on inadequate pensions.
I said I wanted to talk about this thing in terms of three groups of people. I am concerned first of all, anid I think hon. members generally will join with me in this, about those who are now retired and, by the gods of war, Mr. Speaker, we should not let this

session go by without taking action for these people. We failed them in 1967 when a unanimous committee report was brought in by the hon. member for Ottawa East who was chairman of the special joint committee on pensions. In 1968 the story was the same. Now we are in 1969.
[DOT] (12:50 p.m.)
On January 8, 1969, the President of the Treasury Board met with the executive body of the Federal Superannuates National Association on this matter. He assured them there would be a study and he hoped there would be a report in three or four weeks, but two or three months have gone by since then and nothing has come of it. We should not let this question go by without dealing with the case of these people. I am making a plea not only for those who are now retired but also for those who are working in the public service today. These people may be able to compute what their pensions will be on the basis of 70 per cent of their best six years if they have the prospect of obtaining 35 years' service, and it will sound' not bad. The day will come when these people will retire and at the point of retirement things may be all right for them. These people may retire at age 60 after 20 or 25 years' service. Because of longevity and other things they may live until age 85 or 90, but so far as the present arrangements are concerned there will be no increase in their pensions. I contend that we must build into the Public Service Superannuation Act and other pension plans a provision for automatic escalation.
I have pleaded and pleaded that we understand this problem. I did not get it into the head of the Acting Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lang) the other night that we are not concerned only about escalation to meet the rising cost of living but also rising standards. I have a resolution on the order paper which is an attempt to cope with this matter. It provides that public service pensions should be recalculated every year so as to keep them in line with increases in wages and salaries and that, in fact, there should be a relationship between a retired civil servant's pension and the salary attached to the job he had at the time of retirement. This is difficult, new and revolutionary, but unless we do this kind of thing our whole pension program can fall apart and be meaningless, and people will have to fall back on welfare payments of one kind or another.

I have been talking about retired civil servants. I am now talking about those who are working and for whom I think there should be the protection of an escalation clause in the various acts. I am also concerned, however, about the broad sector of the Canadian people. One of the reasons I want the government to act is that I believe it is the government's job to give the lead. We must do the same thing in respect of the old age security pension; we must have an escalation clause tied in with salaries and wages. It is necessary that we give the lead to companies like Canadian National Railways, the Canadian Pacific Railway and other private companies in this country. As the minister knows, because I called it to his attention the other day, many people and bodies now realize that pensions must be on this kind of a basis. Publications like the Financial Post are concerned about this matter. It devoted a whole issue to the problem of keeping pensions in line not just with rising living costs but also with rising living standards.
Those of us who are taking part in this debate today are in effect pleading the case not just of those who are retired civil servants, not just those who are working in the public service and should have something better to look forward to when they retire, but the case of all the retired people of Canada and particularly the case of those who will become retired people. We all get there unless death intervenes. I make the point as strongly as I can that I believe the most important aspect of our pension problem is that we must bring this kind of escalation provision into effect. I appreciate the attention the President of the Treasury Board and his colleague the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cadieux) are paying to my remarks. I think they agree with me. In fact I am sure they agree with me. I believe that even the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), hardhearted though he may be, agrees with me.
The problem is to get started. I am aware that private industry does not want to have to do this. I realize that private industry will be scandalized if the government makes a move like this. Its leaders will say that the government is putting them on the spot. But it is the government's job to give leadership in this field, and I urge as strongly as I can that this be done.
I recall my starting time and I believe I could take five minutes after the luncheon adjournment, but I think I can conclude my remarks now and give the next speaker an
March 14. 1969

Statute Law Amendment Act opportunity to get ready to begin at two o'clock. I should like, however, to take a moment or two to make a few comments which might seem a bit more critical than those I have made up to this point. I have been both pleading and philosophical and have caused the minister's heart to bleed. But I must also say to the government that really the government's record in this matter is disgraceful. All these years-and I have been at it myself for 20 or 25 years-we have been told, as the minister said this morning, that the matter is under active consideration. These pens oners and their widows are dying off at the rate of 150 to 200 a month. I do not know how many have died hearing the last words of the government that an increase in their pensions is under active consideration. This is not good enough.
The whole matter came to a bit of a pitch back in 1966 and 1967 when we pleaded that it be referred to a special joint committee of the House of Commons and the Senate which met at that time under the chairmanship of the hon. member for Ottawa East. There is no doubt in my mind that when the government agreed to have the matter go before the committee it was with the understanding that if the committee came back with a recommendation there would be act on on it. We came back with a recommendation. The present Solicitor General (Mr. Mcllraith), who was house leader at that time, was most helpful on May 18, 1967, and arranged that we have a meeting of the committee that morning so that we could get our report in before prorogation and before the committee would die so that this matter could be dealt with. The report was brought in. I put most of it on the record in speech I made on November 18, 1968, and it is also contained in Votes and Proceedings for May 8, 1967.
Every member of that committee, especially the hon. member for Ottawa East, was of the belief that the step the government had taken carried with it the implication that action would be taken on the report. I am sure the hon. member for Ottawa East would confirm that. I am sure of it myself. In May and June, 1967, I think we were almost there. The then prime minster, Mr. Pearson, assured me several times, as did the present Minister of Finance, that it would be done before the end of June that year, 1967.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are dealing with what I regard as an important proposal in this bill. I do not intend to comment on it in detail. It proposes improvements in various aspects of the superannuation schemes affecting public servants, members of the armed forces and
March 14, 1969

members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Were I to speak on it in detail at this time I could add nothing really to the comments of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) who I am glad to note feels as I do, that this bill represents a significant improvement in all these pension and superannuation plans.
At the risk of perhaps putting myself out of order I should like to comment on the same matter of policy which has been dealt with by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I have in mind the fact that this bill makes no reference to the adjustment of existing pensions of superannuated civil servants and members of the armed forces. I cannot conceal my extreme disappointment that this is the case because this matter is one of long standing. For all practical purposes the starting point in our consideration of this matter should be the recommendations of the special joint committee of the Senate and the House which reported in May of 1967. The text of that committee's report is available to all hon. members and has been referred to in earlier debates in this session by myself and by other hon. members, so I do not think it is necessary to repeat any part of that report in detail or to read it in its verbatim form.
o (2:10 p.m.)
The problem that faces retired civil servants can be summed up best in two ways, I think. First of all, there is the basic problem of equity. People who worked a long time for the government of Canada and did so in the belief that upon their retirement they would be able to maintain a certain standard of life have been disappointed. The reasons for this disappointment include many factors, the chief of which is inflation. T'he value of the pensions which they thought they would be paid upon their retirement has progressively declined because of the devaluation of our currency by persistent and continuing inflation. I am not an economic expert but it seems to me that we must live with the prospect that there will not be a stabilization of the currency and that there will continue to be some degree of inflation in the future. So the first consideration with regard to the position of pensioners is for pensioners in general and the concern which we in parliament should have as the former employers of retired civil servants to ensure that they are fairly treated. Our concern should apply not only during their active years of service but in their years of retirement.
Statute Law Amendment Act
There is a second and, to my mind, even more important consideration which should govern the thinking of hon. members on this subject. There are a number of cases of real hardship among superannuated civil servants. I suppose it is impossible for any government or any parliament to so order its affairs that hardship will not exist in some cases. But we must look at broad categories and at the substantial numbers of people who now suffer hardship. I am sure that all hon. members know very well that in recent years there has been a substantial escalation in the salaries paid to civil servants. Hon. members will also know that pensions are computed on the basis of the salaries which civil servants earned at the time of their retirement. People who may have retired 15 or 20 years ago find that their pensions, which were scaled to the then existing salaries, are very much lower than the pensions of those holding comparable positions in the government who are retiring today. It is in this group that we find the greatest degree of hardship. Many of those people are quite elderly and are forced to subsist on what by any standards must be considered to be a disappointing, and, unhappily in some instances, an abysmally low pension.
Perhaps I have some advantage in speaking in this debate because I am a new member of a new parliament and a supporter of a new government. I do not believe that it is any part of my responsibility to defend actions which may have taken place in the past in parliament. Therefore I propose to make some comments about things which have happened in the past.
It seems to me quite clear that at present we are in a situation which has been brought about by the extravagance of governmental programs, both provincial and federal, and these programs are not only the results of the decisions of whatever governments may have been in power when they were instituted but the results of collective representations and expressions of views of politicians and members of this house in every party. I say quite categorically that everybody bears a major share of responsibility for the problems which are not the problems of the government alone but are in fact the problems of the people of Canada. It is my opinion that at every stage in this parliament we are faced with situations where hard choices have to be made. This is because we have gone almost beyond the outer limits of expenditure in relation to our revenues. Because of the collective result of these decisions of the past,
March 14, 1969

Statute Law Amendment Act this government and this parliament have very little margin in which to manoeuvre and in which to deal with problems such as that ol the retired civil servants.
To me the most heartening part of the address of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) was his statement that the government was now considering this important matter in relation to all the other commitments which the government and this parliament have made to various classes of people in our society, be they old age pensioners or a recipient of any kind of pension, welfare payment and the like. One of the things which attracted me to the support of this government is my belief that it is capable of undertaking the necessary review of the commitments which this parliament and successive governments have made, and as a result of that review establishing policies and priorities for further expenditure which will have some relevance to the future and which will, I hope, contribute materially to the assistance of people who are in the position of retired civil servants.
It is also obvious to all hon. members, and I need hardly mention it, that a statement that this matter is receiving careful consideration is not really of any immediate assistance to the persons now receiving pensions and to people who are now enduring the hardships that I have described. Many of them at their age unhappily have not much longer to live. Apart from that, the people who are struggling and who may be ill find no solace in the suggestion that at some future date relief may be brought to them. Tremendous urgency attaches to the review which must precede the development of policy on this matter.
a (2:20 p.m.)
Notwithstanding all the claims which are made upon the public treasury, and many of them have great merit, special priority and significance should be attached to the position of the retired civil servants. This is because they have been our employees. Whatever may have been the position in the past I believe we in this country have arrived at the view that the obligation of employers to their employees does not cease completely when they retire. There are examples of large firms in industry which recognize a continuing obligation to increase periodically superannuation payments made to their former employees. This principle was recognized in the statute of 1959 and it was firmly endorsed by the

report of the joint parliamentary committee in 1967. To my mind it is now beyond the realm of doubt and of dispute that an obligation of a special kind rests upon the government of Canada as a former employer of these superannuated pensioners to undertake periodic upward adjustment of their pensions in order to provide them with a decent and comfortable standard of life in their retirement.
There are many other things which might be said on this subject. The President of the Treasury Board re-emphasized that there is no magic way in which pensions paid to retired public servants can be increased without a charge on the treasury and ultimately on the taxpayers of Canada. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, in the course of his interesting analysis of the way in which pensions are really paid-I am not saying whether I completely agree with his analysis-made it abundantly clear that ultimately the charge for the payment of pensions falls upon the producing elements of the nation. In the case of pensions paid to retired public servants, for example, this means that unhappily it falls upon the taxpayers. I think it is well for this point to be emphasized because we all live in a situation in which it is generally assumed that taxation has approached something like its ultimate limit, and we must recognize that when we say pensions of retired civil servants should be increased we are not only talking about payment of pensions but we are also talking about the imposition of taxes.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has indicated quite properly the great issues of policy which must be decided when this question of the pensions of retired civil servants is considered. He made it abundantly clear that this matter could not be considered in isolation. One group which he noted in this connection were those in receipt of old age pensions. This indicates to hon. members the magnitude of the collective decision which the government and this parliament utlimate-ly may have to make in relation to any scheme or schemes for the upward adjustment of pensions and payments of this type,
I recognize fully the difficulty encountered by the government in reaching a decision on this very important matter. I applaud my hon. friends on the treasury benches for approaching it in a sensible, constructive and comprehensive way. Frankly, I do not think we could support an ad hoc approach to these and similar problems. Having said all this, I
March 14. 1969

urge the government to accelerate the study which is now in progress and -to take into special consideration the position of its former employees, particularly those whom I regard as suffering a degree of hardship which is not consistent with our view of the way in which people in this society should live.

speechtext:
Then in 1957 it was the same thing again. As reported at page 1859 of Hansard I said:
As I have said before, the civil service of Canada is the best in the world, and because our civil servants are the best they are entitled to the best treatment. I have also said before, and I am not afraid to repeat it, that the government should be the best employer. Although the superannuation act is very good and has been amended often to make it better still, I do not agree that we should base payments of pensions to civil servants entirely upon the contract.
I made another speech in 1958 to the same effect. Then something new happened. Three years ago the old civil service act, what is today the Public Service Superannuation Act, was revised, and toward the end of our work there was a great deal of pressure brought to bear upon the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and myself. Eventually I was asked whether I would stay on as chairman to deal with the superannuated civil servants.
Hon. members can observe my seat in this chamber and see that, I am a sort of lone wolf here. I have some opinions and some judgments and I am not a swinger-in the proper sense, not in the younger sense, of the term. I say what I think and I always think about the same thing. I agreed to become chairman of that committee on one condition, that we would come to a decision which would be seriously acted upon. And I meant seriously; otherwise I would not have been chairman and nobody could have made me chairman had I not wanted to be.
On May 8, 1967, that very excellent committee brought in a report to which reference was made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and the hon. member for Gren-ville-Carleton (Mr. Blair). We had the support of the hon. member for Hull, who had always been very active in the same way as the former hon. member for Ottawa West who is now a minister and has his hands a little more tied than before. Nevertheless, the group of members who formed that committee represented some of the best minds in this house. I was proud of the membership of the committee. It was not at all partisan. As a matter of fact, all of the bills submitted to the committee were amended from top to bottom to suit not one party but the civil service and government relationships therewith generally.
We did not come to the decision that was presented to the house on May 8, 1967, haphazardly. It had involved a great deal of study, it was unanimous, and we thought we

I am in favour of an increase in the pension of those who have worked in the public service of Canada for many years. I share the opinion of those who spoke before me on that subject. Being from the Hull region, we know there are thousands of retired civil servants. The matter has been under consideration in committees for years. A number of hon. members have made representations and the Public Service Alliance of Canada has made claims.
A few years ago, the right hon. Mr. Pearson even informed the vice-president of the Retired Civil Servants Association that some action would be taken in the near future, but nothing has been done yet. In my opinion, these loyal civil servants have served the government and the people of Canada for many years and they certainly deserve to have their pensions increased. Over the past ten years or so, the cost of living has increased by 44 per cent and nothing has been done to increase pensions for these faithful employees.
I would think that these people were not perhaps in a position to serve their country as members of the armed forces during the last war. However, Mr. Speaker, as soldiers were needed on the battlefields, there had to be some people to assist the soldiers on the home front so that victory might be won as soon as

Statute Law Amendment Act
possible and this is what they did. Like the war veterans, they deserve a pension that will permit them to have a standard of living like all other Canadians, in 1969.
These retired civil servants are no doubt entitled to the gratitude of the country for their services. I will always insist that if we must fight for the rights of these pensioners, we will do so because they have been, so to say, the backbone of the country during the last war, serving their country at home while our soldiers were fighting for Canada. I repeat that I will never insist too strongly on this point. I do feel they are entitled to this consideration for the remainder of their life.
I think that it is the responsibility of this house to endorse this policy, to bring the government to an understanding of this problem and to get it to take the necessary measures for an adjustment of the only income received by those retired civil servants for whom I have a great deal of admiration and sympathy.

speechtext:
I listened with a good deal of interest, Mr. Speaker, to the speech of the minister when he introduced this bill. It represents a measure of updating pension legislation, in some cases increasing benefits and in other cases making economic changes which are long overdue. As has been observed by other hon. members, there is little in the bill to which we can take exception. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) said that what was not in the bill gave us more concern than what was in it.
The	last	paragraph of	the	minister'sremarks was a disappointment to me and other hon. members from the national capital region in particular and from other parts of Canada because the government was not able to see its way clear to adjust the pensions of those	who	have retired.	The	minister's
remarks with regard to the interest rate paid on pension funds were particularly illuminating and I listened with interest to what he said in this regard.
One	hon.	member used	the	expression"mythology	of pensions".	Certainly with
regard to the funding provisions and the adjusting of interest rates there is a great deal of confusion. I know there is no confusion in the minds of the minister, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and the other hon. members who have spoken, but many remarks made in this house have led to confusion and a great deal of misunderstanding in other quarters.
The fundamental difference between a publicly operated pension plan and a privately operated pension plan is something academics can discuss at great length. A privately operated plan must be actuarially sound. The Department of Insurance and other supervisory authorities insist on full funding provisions, for which several reasons are given. The same requirements are not always necessary when dealing with public funds because the investment of the sums accumulated involves other questions of public policy. This was discovered during the debate on the Canada Pension Plan.
I do not agree with the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre when he dealt at some length with the question of funding. In effect he said that funding does not matter, the fund does not matter, and all this business about interest rates does not
March 14, 1969

matter. It is true that the adjustment of interest rates to current levels will not produce half of the annual payments of a deficiency nature for arrears of contribution, deferred amortization charges and other items quoted each year in this house. As the minister pointed out, $200 million has been appropriated this year to make up these deficiencies. In my opinion the adjustment of interest rates should have been done some time ago. We have entered into an age of higher interest rates which will continue for at least a generation. This has been forecast by the Economic Council of Canada and there is every reason to believe this forecast. The 4 per cent interest rate level is now seriously out of line. It is the intention of the government to reduce the deficiency payment.
The case of those arguing for an increase in pensions is not aided one bit by talking about the pension fund. No one can look at the income and outgo of a pension fund and talk about whether it is solvent and meeting all actuarial criteria without having an analysis of the fund. That is where actuaries enter into the picture.
I listened to the remarks of the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) for whom I have a high regard. He hoped the committee would study the question of contributions to the fund exceeding the annual outgo. With the greatest of respect to the hon. member, I hope the committee does not waste time doing this. It would be a complete waste of time for the committee to argue with actuaries who have a great deal of technical expertise. The actuaries certainly have the last word over laymen on these matters.
I agree with hon. members on both sides of the house that the case for an adjustment of pensions is basically moral. It is a question of adjusting the standards of living for those who have been affected by inflation over which they have no control. It is a difficult question of public policy, but I believe something will be done about it by the government.
I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, about the misinterpretation of information in this debate. I know hon. members have a clear understanding of what they are saying and I give full marks to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, although he spent more time than I would have on that aspect of his presentation. People listening to this debate, pensioners writing in and those making statements on behalf of the pensioners have given a bad name to a good cause. I have received a substantial number of letters sug-
Statute Law Amendment Act
gesting that I ask the Auditor General to look at the theft that has gone on in the superannuation account. There is no theft, Mr. Speaker. There is no stealing, there is nothing irregular. No contractual obligations have been broken. The law has not been broken in any technical way whatsoever. The excessive preoccupation with the fund has led to the type of arguments' which have given a bad name to those arguing on behalf of pensioners. Every time they talk about the fund they act as though they are actuaries, but they are not. They make statements about the fund which are not true. When they make statements in this way, the proper authorities of government treat them with the seriousness they deserve, even though the cause is a good one.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
The case for an adjustment of pensions is a moral one. It is not a narrow, legal case. It is not a case which can be argued on the basis of a lack of performance, a breach of performance or something of that nature. It is not a case of money that has been stolen, of money that has been misappropriated, of money that has been misapplied. But I receive no end of letters from people in receipt of pensions who have been listening to all this argument about public pension funds and who have come to the conclusion that there is some gross irregularity involved. As a result, they say things that do not help their own cause.
Recently I received a copy of a letter from a man, resident in Florida, that he sent to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and which was grossly insulting to the Prime Minister. The letter contained statements based on his interpretation of what had been done to the fund, and which were a total misconception of what was happening. This kind of argument, this kind of preoccupation with funding, serves no particular purpose.
I hope that at the earliest possible date the government will give consideration to the unanimous recommendations of the committee. I hope it will be able to give consideration to these recommendations at a time when there is a balanced budget, when the kind of fiscal policy which I know the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) is doing his courageous best to establish will have contributed to some degree to the fiscal stability of the country, and stopped inflation.
It is essential that inflation be stopped. If we do not stop inflation, we cannot win by accelerating pensions all down the line. We must bring a halt to inflation through respon-
March 14, 1969

Statute Law Amendment Act
sible fiscal policy. Then, we must take some measures to help restore the standard of living and the equity of those who, through no fault of their own, have placed their savings program in the form of pensions and retirement benefits which have been grossly eroded by inflation.
I repeat that the case is a moral case, but it is no less strong for being moral. Those who speak on behalf of the superannuates in my opinion would be well advised to place their emphasis on the moral side rather than try to set themselves up as actuaries, which they are not.

Mr. Speaker, I think almost enough has been said on this subject by a lot of people who !know an awful lot more about it than I do. Although I was not able to listen to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) and the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), I gather that no one is out of tune with the intent to do well by our old people.
I could not agree more with anybody than I do with the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis) when he said that this was a moral question. This is not a life insurance pension plan type of thing, which is just as well because I would understand it even less if that were the case. However, to me it is a very simple proposition.
No country is an island to itself at any particular moment in history. We come from somewhere, we are going somewhere. In

Canada we have just finished 100 years of work of which I think we can be proud. These people we are talking about have been little people, big people, medium sized people who in a way have handed this country on to us. While we were growing up, while we were learning a few things and getting our minds straight, they were carrying the torch. They have now handed that torch on to us honourably, and by and large it is a pretty good torch. I do not think it is the intention of anyone deliberately to harm these people, but whether that is the intention or not the result is the same.
I find it disgraceful when I go around my constituency and meet an honest, older man, who spent his whole life in the R.C.M.P. Probably because the police force did not encourage marriage, he did not marry until he was relatively old. Now, with all the pensions that he gets he has the munificent sum of $257 a month to provide for his wife and 12 year old child. It is hard for him to sell his 12 year old son on the honesty and integrity of a policeman's job when he sees the way he has been treated by the state at the end of the road. As another example, I mention a man who worked for the Department of Agriculture for years, and who received the munificent retirement pension of $124 a month. Now, he is old enough to get an old age pension in addition to that.
If we are honest with each other and with ourselves, I do not think we can do anything but say that this1 is a disgraceful situation. We have a very high standard of living. We have a fine country. We have been handed the opportunity to make it even finer. If we have $10 million, $15 million or $20 million we can clean up this situation. There must be ways to find $10 million or $15 million to do that. Surely, that amount of money is being spent on less important undertakings.
There is a question of priority and morality involved. Most people admire the retired civil servants, the retired policemen and the retired armed forces people who have handed on the torch of public service to this generation. We should change our order of priorities so that we can look after these people, so that we can enter our second century with a clearer conscience than we have now. I would ask the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) to think long and hard on ways and means of changing priorities so that these people can get a better shake.

Patent Act-Trade Marks Act whole question of drug prices and the related question of the safety of drugs. I recall this because some six or seven years ago I served on a similar committee immediately following what has been known throughout the world as the series of thalidomide tragedies. At that time, the members of the committee were quite concerned about the effect this particular situation might have on the manufacture and sale of drugs. Members from all sides of the house agreed with most of the recommendations made by the committee. Included in those recommendations were a number which dealt with the question of drug safety. I think, so far as our party is concerned, the members who represented this party on the committee took that position but tied to it this question of safety. I have mentioned only the thalidomide situation but there were others which indicated that we must not evade our responsibility here by taking the politically palatable course of saying that prices only would be considered and nothing else; that is, say that we do not consider the question of drug safety to be part of our responsibility here. It may be that if the bill were examined more places could be found in which this provision might be inserted. But we say this effort should not be necessary. The second point raised by the hon. member was that drugs manufactured outside Canada and drugs manufactured inside Canada might be treated in two different ways.
