Patent Act-Trade Marks Act Obviously, this is the case. The manufacture of drugs within this country comes within the legislative competence and control of the parliament of Canada and the process is open to immediate inspection by officials of the food and drug directorate. They have the power to inspect and examine not only the drugs themselves in the laboratories, but the conditions under which they are manufactured. Our officials can examine the ingredients which go into these drugs, the conditions under which they are manufactured and put together, and other factors which influence the production of the drug in its final stage. This is important because it has been admitted many times that the Food and Drug Directorate is unable to cope with the task of inspecting all these drugs. In fact, it has been said the directorate can only conduct spot checks, and that in many cases they are unable to certify quality control.
This has been one of the problems in connection with importing large quantities of drugs. On the other hand, the directorate does have the ability to go to a place of manufacture and inspect not just the end product but the actual facilities used to produce that product. Great concern has been expressed as to the quality of drugs manufactured outside Canada. There have been stories, many of them exaggerated, naturally, of poor quality drugs, drugs of inconsistent quality and drugs manufactured under unsuitable conditions, becoming available to the Canadian market as soon as this bill is passed. The food and drug directorate is not able to inspect the conditions under which they were produced. It can only inspect the end product, and then in a limited way by means of spot checks. For these reasons, there is a good deal of difference between drugs manufactured inside Canada and drugs manufactured outside the country and the only way of ensuring we are protected is, surely, to authorize and provide for the specially careful treatment of drugs manufactured outside Canada.
This subject is of special concern to me, personally. A few months ago I suffered an illness and was placed on a delicate drug in connection with which quality control must be absolute. I know, as a result of my illness, that there is a difference in the quality as between drugs manufactured by one company and another. It is extremely important that there be consistency in the manufacture of many of these drugs so that when a certain

Thus, I have no hesitation in seconding this amendment and no apology to make for doing so. I am aware there is a general theory that one should not deal with one class of persons in a way which discriminates against another in the same field. But here is a situation in which we must do so if the genuine concern of many Canadians and of many members of this house, namely, that there should be rigid quality control over drugs brought into this country, over whose manufacture we have no power of supervision, is to be met.

I share the concern of spokesmen for the Official Opposition in approaching this question of drug safety. However, this subject was carefully and thoroughly considered during the hearings of the Committee on Health and Welfare in connection with the bill before us.
I may say at the outset that my colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro), and I have been careful to separate our different functions and responsibilities under this legislation. Primary authority over the Food and Drug Directorate rests with my colleague, not with myself.
The evidence given before the committee, particularly by Dr. Chapman of the Food and Drug Directorate, showed, I believe, that the directorate does have the authority it requires to deal adequately with the question of the safety of imported drugs. I have in mind clause five which was put into the bill to deal specifically with the question of drug safety by amending the Food and Drugs Act and giving the Food and Drug Directorate the authority to pass regulations dealing with the importation into Canada of any drug or class of drugs manufactured outside Canada. I believe the evidence given before the committee shows the amendment before us to be unnecessary inasmuch as provision for protection has already been made in the bill.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
Other hon. members have pointed out that this amendment also involves another concept, one that I do not think the government or the house should undertake lightly. At the present time responsibility for the safety of drugs rests primarily with the manufacturers of drugs. Through the Food and Drug Directorate, regulations are made pursuant to the Food and Drugs Act, and regulations can be

DEBATES	March 14, 1969
passed pursuant to clause 5. Through its directorate, the government carries out inspections of domestic or imported drugs as the directorate deems necessary in order to ensure that the regulations are complied with.
I think the primary responsibility for the safety of drugs must remain with the manufacturer. To change that onus would, I think, be a very serious step. Therefore, for those two reasons I think the amendment should be opposed.
I might refer also to the evidence given before the health and welfare committee, and I do so in order to state my disagreement with some of the comments of the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken). Evidence was given concerning the increase in the budget of the Food and Drug Directorate, the number of staff positions authorized by Treasury Board for the directorate for their operations in Ottawa and, as their intention is, for service in the United States and Europe.
I disagree with the hon. member that under the act we should look only, as he described it, at the end product. That is not the case, and it is not the intention of the Food and Drug Directorate so to do. The directorate will be able to inspect foreign facilities and the source of manufacturing of imported drugs. If a foreign manufacturer does not cooperate with our inspectors and allow them to inspect the facilities, we will simply not allow importation of that manufacturer's drugs- unless, of course, we are satisfied that the production facilities and techniques are safe.
Therefore, I think that under clause 5 as now worded we have complete authority to deal with importations. We are increasing the staff of the directorate to handle the increased imports. Thirdly, I think that to accept the amendment would create a quite undesirable situation vis-a-vis the manufacturers, who no longer would be primarily responsible for the safety of their products.

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Friday, January 17, consideration of the motion of Mr. LeBlanc (Rimouski) that Bill S-12, respecting The Bonaventure and Gaspe Telephone Company Limited, be read the second time and referred to the standing Committee on Transport and Communications.

maintopic: THE BONA VENTURE AND GASPE TELEPHONE COMPANY, LIMITED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when this bill was last before the house some weeks ago I was speaking and had mot exhausted all the time allotted to me. This afternoon we are discussing Bill S-12, respecting Bonaventure and Gaspe Telephone Company, Limited. Quite a number of hon. members have spoken on the various aspects of the bill. As hon. members know, an attempt is being made under private bills similar to this one to transfer part of our Canadian economy to foreign ownership. Because of the considerable time interval between the various appearances of a bill in its various stages before the house, hon. members lose the thread of debate and may forget points which have been raised with respect to a bill. May I again briefly acquaint hon. members with the over-all picture, as it relates to this particular company. The explanatory note to the bill says that the purpose of it is to resolve doubts as to whether the company may dispose of its undertaking to a company incorporated under or subject to the laws of any province of Canada. But in this explanation too little information is given, not only to hon. members of the house but to Canadian people generally. Also, our citizens know too little generally about what happens in this house with respect to private bills such as this. I shall therefore, speak briefly on the background of this bill.
Oddly, any Canadian looking at the title of the bill would imagine that there we have a small Canadian telephone company. He would not delve too deeply into the widespread ramifications of foreign ownership which flow from the bill. Examining the matter further, we find that the bill deals with a company totally owned by Anglo-Canadian Telephone Company, which in turn is owned by the General Telephone Company. That makes the company in question here a subsidiary of one of the largest telephone companies in the world. In fact, the ultimate parent is one of
IMr. Speaker.]
the largest corporations in the world, with telephone communications systems in Australia, the West Indies, across the United States and, no doubt, in other countries. It is interesting to note that the Anglo-Canadian Company is the counterpart of a number of subsidiary companies under the control of General Telephone and Electronics Corporation. Hon. members will find that to be so if they consult Moody's Public Utility Manual. The latter company really is a holding company with subsidiaries in many countries.
Hon. members should know a little more of the background of this bill if they are to discuss it adequately. In July, 1966, General Telephone purchased Anglo-Canadian Telephone Company and made it a wholly owned subsidiary. They also acquired the controlling interest in Quebec Telephone Company which, at the end of 1967, had about 119,000 telephone subscribers. We find that in 1967 General Telephone, together with a wholly owned subsidiary, Anglo-Canadian Telephone Company, owned over 50 per cent of the British Columbia Telephone Company. It also owned, just over 53 per cent of the Quebec Telephone Company. In 1967, there were 835,000 telephone subscribers in British Columbia.
These facts indicate how the tentacles of the ultimate parent corporation have reached into every section of this nation. What disturbs me most is that in this bill we are dealing with a public utility controlled by someone who does not live in our country. Where do we stop in giving away the ownership of our assets to foreigners?
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
I believe that many utilities, such as the telephone service, ought rightfully to be monopolies. It will be extremely costly for the community to have rival telephone companies operating in the same territory. Since by its vary nature a telephone operation lends itself to monopoly control, such, operation ought to be controlled by the people it serves, who in this case happen to be the people of Canada. Any government, individual or party fostering, advocating and assisting in removing from our national control such public utilities is, to be perfectly frank, doing a great disservice to our nation. It is therefore amazing to see members of the government party in this house sponsoring bills of this type. If it is government policy for them to do so, let that government policy be announced. Let government supporters go to
March 14, 1969

the Canadian people at election time and say, "Here, we will sell you out, lock, stock and barrel." I am disappointed to see through the medium of private bills similar to this one that come before this house little chunks of Canada's economy going on the auction block week after week. I sometimes wonder what private members the government benches think of this. They should be able to see what is happening and take a stand in their ridings, party and caucus. There should be a clearcut program and policy on liquidation, 'as in this particular instance, of public utilities in this country. I have raised this point before and will continue to raise it. There have been warnings galore. I do not know how many hon. members have read and studied in detail the report of the task force on the structure of Canadian industry. This report is entitled "Foreign Ownership and the Structure of Canadian Industry". The short title is, The Watkins Report.
This report sets out in detail what is happening to Canada and Canadian industry. This report, ocmmissioned by this government to give direction to it warns that the control of our Canadian economy is going by the board. At the start of the first session of the news parliament in 1968 the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) stated there would be a new deal for Canadians. What has happened? Private member after private member on the government side introduced private bills which placed another chunk of Canada's economy on the auction block. People from one end of the country to another should know what individual members are trying to do to Canada's economy. Once they get away from their constituencies, they do not report to their constituents what they are trying to do. That is why we are raising this issue, Mr. Speaker, and will continue to raise it.
Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That Bill S-12 be not now read a second time, but that it be read a second time this day six months hence.

maintopic: THE BONA VENTURE AND GASPE TELEPHONE COMPANY, LIMITED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if as was shown by the previous speaker, there is great doubt as to the legality of this bill, giving it the six months' hoist might not be a bad thing. The Bonaventure and Gaspe Telephone Compnay Limited cannot be in such a hurry to sell that it cannot wait another six months.
Private Bills
As far as private bills related to companies are concerned, one cannot always depend more than necessary upon the decisions of the Canadian Transport Commission, which in the last analysis must approve or disapprove of the sale of a company, as the case here. It follows from that that we already have proofs that monopolies were created to the knowledge of the commission.
I will give you an example, in the information and telecommunication field, of a company such as the Power Corporation, that has succeeded more or less in exercising an information monopoly through several newspapers in the province of Quebec as well as quite a number of radio and television stations. Such monopolies may present a real danger to democracy, which proves that one is never too cautious in that field.
The fact remains however that this bill seems to protect freedom well enough. One may be inclined to say at first blush that the company has indeed the right to do what it wants. But when one knows the extraordinary power of trusts, of certain financial sharks, one is forced to act as a watch-dog and to sound the alarm. That is the reason why I support the motion to defer consideration of this bill for six months from today.

maintopic: THE BONA VENTURE AND GASPE TELEPHONE COMPANY, LIMITED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to give my impressions and comment on some of the remarks made on the motion that has just been presented.
Unless I am mistaken, a while ago the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Hardin) insisted on the fact that the owners of the company concerned in this bill are foreigners. If such is the case, I cannot but share his opinion, in theory as well as in practice.
I also heard our hon. friend, the member for Champlain (Mr. Matte) point out the harmful effects of some monopolies and trusts; if such is the case, he is right.
Mr. Speaker, allow me to put forward a few details which I hope will help to refute the assertion that foreigners control the Quebec Telephone Company. First of all, according to my information which I believe is as credible as that of my hon. friends of the opposition, all the shares of the Bonaventure and Gaspe Telephone Company Limited are owned by the Quebec Telephone Company, with the exception of those which are known as directors' qualifying shares, and three or four others which are owned by an American estate. Furthermore, Quebec Telephone is the

March 14. 1969
Private Bills
sole creditor and it alone finances the development oi the Bonaventure and Gaspe Telephone Company because the financial situation of the latter is such that it is unable to obtain funds on the money market at a reasonable rate.
The Quebec Telephone Company, if my information is correct, has over 3,000 shareholders of whom a large number are Canadian citizens. However, I have been advised that the Sogibry, a Canadian company, had sold 51 per cent of its shares to the Anglo-Canadian Telephone Company, which has held a Quebec charter since about 1934, which also owns 51 per cent of the shares of the British Columbia Telephone Company, that holds a federal charter.
Someone said that steps were to be taken to grant a Canadian charter to the American company, the General Telephone Company, which, in my opinion, is impossible.
There is one other point I should like to make, though I do not want to unduly extend the debate. Out of the 600 telecommunications companies in Canada, only three hold a federal charter: The Bell Telephone Company, The British Columbia Telephone Company, and the small company the present bill is dealing with, the Bonaventure and Gaspe Telephone Company Limited.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
All three companies, moreover, are registered with the Canadian Stock Exchange in Montreal and Toronto. My hon. friends of the opposition have the right to go and buy the securities of these private companies and to have a share in their profits.
I just ask them to give us a chance of having this bill considered in committee. I am very much concerned by the fact that the Canadian citizens-most of whom, because of their daily activities, are not quite aware of what is going on in parliament-realize that we have been going on for months, nay, for years, repeating the same things on the same subject.
We will all be charged-not only the government members, but also the opposition members-with inefficiency and with misusing our parliamentary institutions.
It would be so easy-and so sensible-to have this bill deferred to the committee. If, later on, we felt we should oppose the bill, we would have plenty of opportunities to vote for or against it. We could at least do ourselves the justice of having acted as sensible

people, giving the matter thorough consideration. And why?
Because-and this seems to be a platitude that we must often repeat in the house-the witnesses, the people concerned, the official representatives of these companies will have answered our questions.
Before I conclude my remarks, I would like to recall that a few years ago, the newspapers reported that the Sogibry Company was selling its stock to an American company. That was not the case since a great amount of the stock is still in the hands of Canadian citizens.
We know that the area serviced by this company is regarded, rightly or wrongly, as an underdeveloped area. It was chosen as a pilot area. And our citizens, rightly or wrongly, often feel neglected by the big cities like Montreal, which are located far from the Gaspe area and forget about its people. That could well be one of the reasons for their living in poverty.
We know that there is in Quebec a small group of young and not so young people that are called separatists. We find them mainly in the big cities that I have just named, and my compatriots of the Lower St. Lawrence and Gaspe areas keep on saying that we are neglected and that these separatists also forget about us. But, when it is a question of hurting us in one way or another, then they do not forget us.
I remember that one day, a few separatists from Montreal insisted very strongly in the newspapers and through other means to prevent this transaction which all the people of our area wanted. Why? Precisely because it meant progress for the people of our area. And we know what discussions had been going on at that time. It was a question of the sale of Quebec Telephone to another Canadian company of which we are proud. Besides, our citizens feared that the administration of this company would be transferred somewhere else, which was possible. Indeed, the Quebec Telephone has several hundreds of employees who contribute to the economic development of our area. The transaction was done and the personnel remained with us. Moreover, this enabled two very important factories to get established in one of the areas that were designated by the government.
If this bill were passed, this small company which serves a small population and has at
March 14, 1969

the most 13,000 subscribers would save $100,000 a year. Furthermore, if my computation is correct, the government of Canada could recover in taxes about $52,000 a year. By leaving things as they are now the federal government loses $1,000 a week.
Earlier, I was referring to separatism. I ask some hon. members whose views I respect not to play the game of those separatists who tried to hurt our people, and to call the representatives of the company so as to make sure that this transaction will help the small people of Gaspe, especially the citizens of the Bonaventure and Gaspe ridings.
It is fine to state great principles and I am for that but before doing so, I think that it would be a good idea to consider their effects.
Mr. Speaker, before closing I ask my friends to behave in such a way as to give the Canadian people the impression that we are taking our job seriously and that our discussions are not just some sort of entertainment. At this stage I would ask the hon. members of the opposition to co-operate so this bill be referred to a committee, then if our friends who are objecting to it have serious reasons to do so-they will have an opportunity to make their point. When they object that these companies' interests are held by foreigners and that we might be building a great monopoly-as was mentionned by the hon. member for Champlain-I could reply that if the bill is referred to the committee, they will have every opportunity to get information.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the citizens of the Gaspe area I ask our friends who object to this bill to enable us to meet the representatives of the company so that we can look into this matter in great detail. Then, come what may, everyone will be free to vote according to his own views.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)

Mr. Speaker, before the member takes his seat, perhaps I might ask him a question. I was very interested in his presentation, particularly in the light of the fact that he represents the area in question. I have no disagreement with his contention that the Gaspe has been neglected. But is he not aware that with the passage of this bill this company, in effect, would pass from the control of the federal government and the Department of Transport which now sets the rates. The rate structure would then be left

free to be established by Quebec Telephone rather than by the federal Department of Transport. This, obviously, would have some effect on the telephone service in his area.

maintopic: THE BONA VENTURE AND GASPE TELEPHONE COMPANY, LIMITED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will first answer my hon. friend's question in a general way. The first object of the present bill is to *authorize a sale. In the second place, it is intended precisely to improve services in accordance with technological changes and developments in the field of communications.
At the present time, this small company which exists in name only cannot improve its own situation, develop normally.
With regard to rates, I must honestly admit that I would not be in a position to give an exact answer. I think those who will appear before the committee will be in a position to answer those questions more accurately than I could do so myself.
As I said, one of the objectives of the present bill is to improve services.

maintopic: THE BONA VENTURE AND GASPE TELEPHONE COMPANY, LIMITED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I was extremely interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. LeBlanc). Naturally, I am very interested in his side of this particular question. Since he is the member from this area, he has a particular interest in this company. I would not quarrel with that at all. I know that if this were a small telephone company in my riding I would be vitally interested in it and would be working very hard to see that service in that particular area was improved.

maintopic: THE BONA VENTURE AND GASPE TELEPHONE COMPANY, LIMITED
speechtext: We would not be against it.

maintopic: THE BONA VENTURE AND GASPE TELEPHONE COMPANY, LIMITED
speechtext:
Certainly, I would not assume that if I were for something in my riding the members of the government would be against me because I believe some members, at least those from New Brunswick, are very generous and would not necessarily be against something because I happen to be for it. I apologize to the hon. member for Rimouski because I am unable to reply to his representations in his own language. I feel that is my fault and I apologize for it.
The hon. member discussed the ownership of this particular company. When I first spoke on this bill on December 3, I too, since I was a rather new member, was perhaps a bit naive

March 14. 1969
Private Bills
about this situation. I did not see the connection between this little company in Gaspe and various other companies not only in this country but also in the United States. The Financial Post recently conducted a survey and issued a report. I should like to read from the speech of the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) of December 3, as recorded at page 3444 of Hansard. I shall read part of this into the record because I believe it is important:
The report tells us that a subsidiary of Quebec Telephone Is the Bonaventure and Gaspe Telephone Company, which is wholly owned and serves the south shore of the Gaspe Peninsula, Quebec. So this is the first link in the chain of ownership. We then set about further investigation and found that Quebec Telephone is itself a subsidiary of the Anglo-Canadian Telephone Company whose head office is situated at 715 Victoria Square, Montreal. This is a holding company whose subsidiaries own telephone systems in British Columbia, Quebec and the Dominican Republic, and supervise publication of telephone directories and installation of services for telephone companies in Canada. The company is itself a subsidiary of General Telephone and Electronics Corporation which acquired all of its class A shares in 1965 through an exchange offer of two and a half General Telephone shares for each class A share of Anglo-Canadian.
Then, this report lists the various directors and ultimately we have a mixture of Canadian and United States directors. The ownership eventually falls into the hands of United States interests. This is something about which members of our party have continuously been concerned. I know members on the Other side of the house are becoming very dreary of our particular stand on this matter. We believe, however, that it is important to bring to public attention a situation which we in this party-I know this view is shared by a great number of Canadians-feel is constantly eroding Canadian ownership in vital utilities and financial institutions, and causing it to fall into foreign hands. I think this is something about which we must be very careful.
I, too, like the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Harding), am very concerned when this sort of thing happens under the guise of something else. We do not believe it really is to the credit of any government member to assist in this particular development. Only the other night Mr. Watkins, the author of the famous Watkins report which has to do with the structure and ownership of Canadian business, said in Toronto that it is almost too late to recoup a major portion of Canadian industry, natural resources and financial institutions which is in foreign hands. This almost makes this parliament irrelevant. We know the government has accepted the Watkins report. So

far I have seen no move on the part of the government to implement any of its recommendations. This is a very important report because it not only implies a loss of our economic sovereignty but ultimately the loss of our political sovereignty. Many Canadians are concerned because decisions that relate to this country are being made by people outside our borders. This should not be the case so long as we have a country that maintains its sovereignty and a particular identity.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
Let us think of the amount of money we devote each year to the various schemes and functions of the communications media, the C.B.C. and other operations in order to preserve our Canadian identity. This is the taxpayers' money that is being spent to preserve the Canadian identity on the one hand, yet on the other hand we give away control of our economy. If we continue to do this, we are going to lose this race.
Perhaps this loss of Canadian sovereignty is not so important. It seems to me if we are going to maintain a viable and clearly independent Canada a greater number of people must concern themselves with this situation. The people in this federal house are the ones who should be most interested in this. The members of this party will not be party to any such move. We will fight any move coming before the house during the private members hour or at 'any other time which assists, aids or abets this kind of thing.
Yesterday afternoon the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Deachman) got very upset. He delivered a highly emotional testimonial. He made a very good speech and I compliment him upon it. I think he showered more heat than light on the subject. Nevertheless, I compliment him for his oratorical ability. In any event, we are going to fight these moves and no one will dissuade us.
Let me also say to the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra that we are not the only people who use a great deal of time which might be considered unnecessary by hon. members in some quarters of the house in talking out the private members hour. I can think of many good bills, private and public, that have been presented to the house. I think I have agreement in this respect from all sides of the house. When this occurs the members on the government side talk-out these bills. I think members on this side of the house are equally guilty in this regard. I have expressed my opinion on more than one
March 14, 1969

occasion about the futility of the private members hour.
We must be very concerned about problems in respect of big corporations or multi-national corporations. It is not necessarily so that what is good for General Motors is good for the country. I do not believe that. Virtually every country in the western world has taken steps which have advanced their economic sovereignty. If we are going to maintain any economic independence, we have to do something.
We have been amassing luxuries. This is the result of our being tied to continentalism. The matter does not stop there. The Gaspe company is not just a little company. It has links with a United States corporation. The British Columbia Telephone Company in my province is in exactly the same position. The existence of these multi-national corporations is a relatively new phenomenon which is not limited to Canada or the United States. Certainly, the concept of multi-national corporations is in existence in Europe, Asia and South America, although it is relatively new. We do not really know how to deal with these problems. Very few people have faced up to this issue or studied the effects of it. They have very little to recommend as to how to deal with it.
Certainly, a multi-national corporation has no political or ideological roots. You cannot say, on the one hand, that these corporations are the result of free enterprise when you realize that on the other hand they are much more powerful than governments. It seems to me also that we need business, investment and the kind of thing which will create jobs. If we are sincere in terms of maintaining our sovereignty and political freedom we had better be very careful about what is happening. I, personally, am sorry to see a member of the government supporting a bill such as this. Perhaps the kind of nationalism I am talking about is an outdated concept.
When I went to high school 20 or 30 years ago I was told that nationalism was responsible for all kinds of things; wars, economic disaster, political and social breakdown, and that perhaps the boundary lines separating nations should disappear. As yet we do not have any adequate substitute for nationalism, but whether we like it or not we should be looking for new political structures and administrative units. Perhaps the kind of thing that is happening now represents a step in the right direction, whether we like it or not.
Private Bills
In spite of the fact that all my high school teachers told me that nationalism was outdated, I am prepared to suggest that if they thought about it now they would come to the conclusion they were wrong. The ideology of this particular century, certainly from the 1950's, the 1960's and since World War II, has been nationalism. We see this happening in Africa and in Asia. These are small administrative units and small political units. The tragedy which is taking place in Nigeria is an example of this. We have even seen nationalism coming about in Britain in the concept of one rule for Scotland. We can see the spectre of separatism in Quebec. I would be very sorry if this type of thing occurred. I hope that when someone from French Canada comes out to British Columbia he will look around and say: This is my country. When I go across the river northward into Quebec, that is what I want to be able to say. If separatism reaches the stage where people are forced into any other position I will be very sorry.
We have not found solutions to problems of this kind. Many suggestions have been made on a national basis. The hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. LeBlanc) made the statement that separatism in relation to the kind of thing that the people in his riding were concerned about can be considered vis-a-vis the problems in Montreal. I am sure the people who are most critical would not feel very comfortable if they realized the true nature of the comparison between this little telephone company in Gaspe and perhaps the General Telephone and Telecommunications Company of the United States.
The diversified multi-national corporation concept is a situation we must deal with realistically. I do not think we are unique or the only country facing this kind of new technique. We had a private members hour yesterday and we heard testimony and evidence to suggest that our financial institutions were being increasingly dominated by foreign interests. This has caused particular difficulty for Canadians. We are experiencing a time of inflation, and we do not control our own financial institutions. How can we really be responsible for priorities, and how can we create those things we need in this country?
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
These institutions lend money to governments. The government of Canada must go to them for the funds which it needs. These companies invest in things that bring the

March 14. 1969
Private Bills
highest return, so currently they are certainly not investing in municipal bonds which might assist in capital works. We all know that the bond market is in a bad state. These companies are not interested in it. We do not control them, so there is no money for bonds and consequently there is no money for capital works. There is also no money for housing because these companies invest only in mutual stocks and shares from which they can get a large return.
I think we should look into that problem very thoroughly because we will have to come up with legislation to overcome it. Encouragement to institutions such as mortgage loan companies by the Minister of Transport is not going to be enough. We will have to say to them: "So much of your money must go into mortgage money for homes".
Such multinational corporations as the Gaspe Company and General Telephone and Telecommunications are only two of many, but there will be fewer and fewer of them if they grow larger and larger. One of the men who has given a great deal of attention to this problem is the noted economist, John K. Galbraith. He discussed the problems of our future as they relate to bigness in his book called "The New Industrial State". In it, he outlined various features of our society which I will run through rapidly. An increasing amount of time is necessary for new products to be put on the market. There is a diminution of a micro-fraction of the tasks to be performed. Great increases of capital are necessary for anything to be produced, and once the plans are laid there is an inflexibility so far as change is concerned. We cannot make changes rapidly enough. Specialized manpower is needed, and so is a huge bureaucratic organization to put any new product on the market. A great deal of planning and arranging is needed, as well as market stimulation brought about by advertising. The stimulation of want is not what we need any more. We are told what we want through advertising.
We have been very successful in our kind of society, probably more successful than any other previous age or civilization but, as Galbraith states, what counts is not the quantity of goods but the quality of our life. We are constantly faced with the growing alienation of the young-we see this in universities, but not only there. We see this in the dropouts of our society, the hippies, the yippies and the lippies. They are alienated because they do
[Mr. Rose.l
not really have any part in this system which is above and beyond them.
I think it is the responsibility of members of parliament to bring this problem to the attention of everyone, but especially to those people who feel that nobody really cares. Parliament has become irrelevant to a great many people, as I found during the last electoral campaign when people said they were not going to vote. When I asked them why, they answered: "What difference does it make?"
The problem of these large industrial multinational corporations is receiving a great deal of attention. Today I received in the mail a notice from the Canadian Chamber of Commerce. The members of my party will pardon me if I read from this document. In it they are announcing their 73rd annual meeting in Puerto Rico on March 14. I certainly hope that the wives of the members attending this business meeting will have the privilege of subtracting their expenses from their income tax. The topic of the meeting is "Productivity Trends and the Multinational Corporation". So other people are becoming concerned, especially the business world, and find it important to study this particular problem. I think we also should be concerned about this problem, especially as it relates to our country, our sovereignty, our political freedom and our identity.
I would like to conclude by saying that our telephone system in Canada has a virtual monopoly in our communications system and it is largely dominated by interests residing outside our national borders. In spite of this we spend millions of dollars every year on the C.B.C. We do all kinds of things to increase our Canadian identity, but we are content to give into hands other than our own this vital link in our communications network. I think this process must be stopped. We must take a determined stand to ensure that it does not happen. Let us consider what is happening with our radio stations. I have here a bulletin from the Broadcasting League which names some 21 stations owned by one man. If I had time I would name them all, but I will spare hon. members this. Our concern about this problem is important because of the opportunity which the communications media have for making propaganda and swaying public opinion to buy and sell certain things. We cannot adopt a laissez-faire attitude with regard to this.
March 14, 1969
I have tried to outline broadly some of the concerns shared by me, by my party, and also, I hope, by members on the other side of the house, about the trend that is taking place in the business world of our country with regard to the ownership of our country. I may not say it as emotionally as have some people, but that does not mean that I am any the less concerned. I certainly think that a committee should study this bill, but-
